OPERATIVE executes bounded work within NORMATIVE rules and standards.

Packages assembled from accepted upstream truth but not themselves authoritative decomposition truth are derivative packages.
Regenerated KTY-local artifacts, _Aggregation outputs, hypergraph snapshots, audit snapshots, concordance packages, and publication packages are derivative packages.
Derivative packages must cite their accepted upstream snapshots.
Derivative packages must not be treated as substitutes for decomposition truth.
Every phase-boundary decision that changes or validates governed state must terminate in a new immutable snapshot.
Pointer updates are permitted only where the owning workflow explicitly allows them.
Later phases consume accepted snapshots rather than relying on mutable working state alone.
Workflows that stop with work intended for another agent or later phase must emit an explicit handoff state.
Handoff state must name accepted upstream snapshots, derivative-package status, closure verdict, rerun requirements, and remaining blockers.
A scope unit or phase is not closed merely because files were written.
Closure requires authoritative truth to be accepted.
Closure requires required derivative packages to be regenerated or explicitly deferred.
Closure requires audit status to be recorded.
Closure requires unresolved blockers to be surfaced in the handoff state.
Later phases that consume derivative packages must run only after upstream authoritative snapshots have been accepted.
Required handoff state must record which derivative packages are current before later phases consume derivative packages.

The document identifies Chirality AI Ltd. as document issuer metadata.
The document records issue date and revision metadata for the Chirality Framework.
The Chirality Framework is a theory of professional accountability with AI agent systems.
The Chirality Framework is the theoretical foundation for the Chirality agent operating system and its professional practice.
The framework explains knowledge in AI-assisted professional work, the architecture that meaning requires, and what remains irreducibly human.
The framework is not a total theory of agency, politics, or knowledge in every setting.
The framework addresses professional accountability within knowledge work: what may be relied on, by whom, on what grounds, and under what commitment.
The framework is broader than the technical definition of an agent and narrower than a complete metaphysics of human action.
The framework underlies the four-pillar design philosophy, epistemic architecture, and regulatory integration.
The framework was developed to explain, organize, and discipline an architecture shaped by recurrent failure modes in real deliverable work.
The framework does not claim that the architecture was derived from theory alone.
In professional practice, knowledge is not a property of information.
Professional knowledge is a relationship between a claim, a warrant, and an accountable person.
A claim is an assertion that something is the case.
A warrant is the justification for believing a claim, grounded in evidence.
An accountable person is a qualified professional who commits to a claim on the basis of the warrant under duty of care.
A claim without a warrant is assertion.
A warrant without an accountable person is evidence.
An accountable person without inspectable grounds is unsupported faith.
Claim, warrant, and accountable person must all be present and inspectable for professional knowledge to exist.
Professional knowledge is something a competent person warrants under duty of care, backed by an auditable record.
Information becomes knowledge when an accountable professional warrants it.
Processing, retrieval, or verification does not automatically transform information into knowledge.
The transition from information to knowledge is an act of commitment.
A professional turns information into knowledge by examining the claim, assessing the warrant, and accepting responsibility for the result.
An AI system cannot perform the act of commitment that turns information into knowledge.
AI agents can produce claims, attach warrants, and classify the epistemic status of claims.
AI agents cannot supply the accountable person.
The gap between information and knowledge is the space in which professional responsibility lives.
Professional authentication is a double commitment rather than a single act of acceptance.
The inner commitment affirms that work-product claims are warranted, evidence supports them, and each claim status is understood.
The outer commitment affirms that the professional is bound to the stance through professional standing, seal, and personal accountability.
Both inner and outer commitment are required for professional authentication.
A professional who reviews claims without committing to the result has not authenticated.
A professional who commits without reviewing has not warranted.
The architecture must make every claim warrant state inspectable for the inner commitment.
The architecture must bind the professional act of acceptance to specific identified content for the outer commitment.
The framework is named for a structural property of knowledge itself.
Chirality is the property of a molecule whose mirror image cannot be superimposed on the original.
Professional knowledge is composed of complementary, non-superimposable components whose pairing is constitutive.
Claim and warrant are chiral: a claim asserts, while a warrant justifies.
Claim and warrant are both required for knowledge, and neither can be derived from the other.
Meaning and commitment are chiral: meaning is encountered in the work, while commitment is enacted through authentication.
Meaning does not produce commitment, and commitment does not compensate for absent meaning.
Content and accountability are chiral: informational structure is one hand, and the responsible professional is the other.
Knowledge exists only when content and the responsible professional are present and bound together.
The chirality of professional knowledge is not a limitation to resolve; it is the structure that makes knowledge possible.
If claim and warrant collapsed, grounded assertions could not be distinguished from ungrounded assertions.
If meaning and commitment were derivable from each other, professional decision would not be needed.
If content and accountability were superimposed, there would be no space for warranting.
The architecture makes both hands of knowledge visible, while the professional holds them together.
The seal binds the chiral pair by declaring that content was inspected, warrant assessed, and responsibility accepted.
The semantic algebra formalizes chirality through Matrix A and Matrix B as non-superimposable inputs.
Neither Matrix A nor Matrix B alone generates the semantic space; the algebra brings both hands together.
The framework uses agent in a bounded technical sense within a larger accountability structure.
In Chirality runtime, an agent is a controlled system architecture of model, instructions, file access, and tool use.
In regulated practice, an AI agent is also one of the others whose work a licensed professional relies on.
The technical and professional definitions of agent operate at different levels rather than competing.
The technical definition explains what an artificial agent is and how it acts.
The professional definition explains how an artificial agent work product is governed, reviewed, and relied upon.
Artificial agents have bounded operative agency but not accountable agency.
Artificial agents can produce claims, attach warrants, surface gaps and conflicts, and act within constrained write scopes.
Artificial agents cannot accept duty of care, authenticate work products, or assume professional consequences of error.
Humans and AI agents participate in the same workflow but not in the same mode.
The difference between humans and AI agents is a difference of responsibility, not merely capability.
A system of many agents arranged into bounded roles, gates, dependencies, and handoffs becomes a form of project management.
Folder structure, stable identifiers, decomposition, lifecycle states, dependency records, gate reviews, and change controls coordinate professional work.
In Chirality, coordination structures are the filesystem itself rather than a separate management layer.
Chirality deliberately couples project structure and epistemic structure.
The project state makes inspectable what exists, what is being worked on, what is known, what is unresolved, and what may proceed.
Chirality distinguishes normative, operative, and evaluative functions.
Normative functions define rules and standards.
Operative functions execute within rules and standards.
Evaluative functions assess, audit, reconcile, and judge.
Governance requires authority, execution, and review to be related without collapsing into undifferentiated power.
Project governance and political governance share a recurrent grammar where responsible action is organized under inspectable authority.
Professional knowledge work cannot be separated from agency, organization, and governance.
A person cannot determine what to rely on without knowing who acted, under what constraints, through what process, and under whose authority.
The framework addresses the transition from information to warranted reliance in work that carries professional consequences.
The framework contains accounts of agents, teams, and governance but is reducible to none of them.
The framework is concerned with agents, teams, and governance only insofar as they bear on accountable knowledge.
The normalization table keeps the framework distinctions compactly in view.
An AI agent is an artificial operative actor that may produce claims, attach or record warrants, and classify epistemic status.
An AI agent may not issue rulings, authenticate for reliance, or bear professional responsibility.
A licensed professional is an accountable person under duty of care who may produce claims, record warrants, classify status, issue rulings, authenticate, and bear responsibility.
A claim is an epistemic primitive that receives classification but does not issue rulings, authenticate, or bear responsibility.
A warrant is an epistemic primitive that does not produce claims, issue rulings, authenticate, or bear responsibility.
A ruling is a binding human decision that may cite grounds, issues rulings, and bears responsibility through the responsible human.
A work product or deliverable is an informational artifact that contains claims, contains warrants, and carries aggregate epistemic state.
A work product does not authenticate for reliance until authenticated by a human.
Warranting requires inspectability, and inspectability must be architectural rather than aspirational.
A system that recommends transparency is a guideline.
A system that makes opacity structurally impossible is a governance framework.
If a professional cannot inspect an element, they cannot warrant it.
If a professional cannot warrant an element, knowledge does not exist.
The architecture must make every element of the warranting act inspectable.
Professional accountability requires four questions to be answered wherever a person takes responsibility for work.
Ontology asks what exists and requires inspectable entities, identifiers, state, and relationships in the work.
Epistemology asks what is warranted and requires inspectable claims, evidence, certainty status, and gaps.
Praxiology asks how the work was done and requires inspectable processes, boundaries, authorities, and execution history.
Axiology asks what values governed and requires inspectable principles, constraints, and professional obligations that shaped decisions.
Ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology form a compact structure for professional accountability.
The four pillars provide an evaluative lens for systems that aim to support informed professional responsibility.
Without ontology, the professional does not know what they are responsible for.
Without epistemology, the professional does not know what to believe.
Without praxiology, the professional does not know how the work was performed.
Without axiology, the professional does not know why decisions were made as they were.
Ontology and epistemology form the structural chiral pair of what exists and what is warranted about what exists.
Praxiology and axiology form the action chiral pair of how work is done and what values govern it.
Ontology without epistemology is structure without knowledge of what the structure means.
Epistemology without ontology has nothing to attach warrants to.
Praxiology without axiology is execution without purpose.
Axiology without praxiology is values without enactment.
The complete framework requires both chiral pairs, and neither pair can be superimposed on the other.
Epistemology is the load-bearing pillar of the Chirality architecture.
Ontology, praxiology, and axiology are necessary but exist in service of epistemology.
Ontology gives the epistemic architecture something to operate on.
Praxiology enforces the epistemic architecture through bounded execution and human gates.
Axiology anchors the epistemic architecture in professional responsibility.
Epistemology is load-bearing because it governs the warrant that determines whether professional commitment is grounded or empty.
The epistemology has a formal domain model with six primitives that constitute the epistemic layer.
A claim is the atomic unit: every non-trivial assertion produced by an agent in a governed workflow.
A warrant is always extrinsic justification for believing a claim, such as a source citation, never model confidence or plausibility.
Status is the epistemic classification of a claim certainty as FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, or TBD.
A gap is an explicit positive assertion that a warrant has not been found.
A gap represents absence of information as a visible and actionable entity rather than silent omission.
A conflict is two or more claims with incompatible warrants about the same key.
A conflict is an entity that must be resolved through a ruling.
A ruling is a human decision that resolves a gap or conflict, transforms epistemic status, and is binding in versioned files.
A claim has a status.
A claim may have a warrant.
A claim without a warrant is a gap.
An unwarranted claim is marked TBD or remains an uncited PROPOSAL.
Two claims may be in conflict.
A conflict requires a ruling.
A ruling transforms status.
FACT means a directly observed claim with citation.
ASSUMPTION means an inferential claim grounded in cited material that still requires validation.
PROPOSAL means a suggested interpretation, action, or design move requiring human decision before becoming binding.
TBD means an explicit placeholder for missing information or missing warrant.
A TBD is a visible gap, not a silent omission.
The epistemic ontology is enforced through four mechanisms that make epistemic failure structurally detectable.
Mandatory provenance makes inspectable whether every claim has a warrant, source citation, or explicit location TBD.
No invention makes missing data visible as TBD instead of plausible fabrication.
Conflict surfacing exposes contradictions with competing sources instead of silently resolving them.
Epistemic labeling makes every claim carry FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, or TBD.
The system does not prevent epistemic failures; it makes them impossible to hide.
Claims within a work product progress through a lifecycle that tracks their epistemic state.
The warrant lifecycle progresses from UNWARRANTED to CITED to REVIEWED to AUTHENTICATED.
UNWARRANTED means a claim exists without a source citation and has TBD status or uncited PROPOSAL status.
CITED means a claim has a source citation and status FACT, ASSUMPTION, or cited PROPOSAL, but no professional has committed to it.
REVIEWED means a professional has examined the claim, assessed its warrant, and dispositioned findings.
AUTHENTICATED means the professional has bound themselves to the work and completed the double commitment.
An authenticated claim is part of a professionally warranted work product.
The warrant lifecycle is interleaved with the production lifecycle of the work product.
A deliverable in progress contains claims in varying warrant states.
A deliverable is ready for issuance when the professional determines its aggregate warrant state is sufficient for reliance.
Thorough review is the operational process of auditing warrant sufficiency.
During review, the professional examines claims, checks warrants, resolves gaps and conflicts through rulings, and determines whether authentication is supported.
The four pillars appear at every level of the system.

At the governance-document level, TYPES and SPEC express ontology, CONTRACT and SE Analysis express epistemology, DIRECTIVE and PROFESSIONAL_ENGINEERING express axiology, and DBM and agent protocols express praxiology.

At the agent-instruction level, header blocks express ontology, invariants and provenance rules express epistemology, non-negotiable constraints express axiology, and protocol sections express praxiology.
At the production-document level, datasheets express ontology, specifications express epistemology, guidance expresses axiology, and procedures express praxiology.
Chirality repeats the four pillars because it must answer the same accountability questions at every level of abstraction.
The fractal property is evidence that the same accountability logic is carried through governance documents, agent instructions, and production documents.
The fractal property is the chirality of knowledge recurring at every system level.
Knowledge in a deliverable, agent instruction, or governance document is composed of complementary non-superimposable components whose pairing is constitutive.
The same chiral structure appears at every level because knowledge at every level has the same structural property.
Classical systems engineering disciplines emerge as mechanisms for operationalizing the four-pillar commitments in Chirality.
Ontology as stable inspectable state leads to architecture, structural design, and configuration management.
Epistemology as evidence-first auditable knowledge leads to verification and validation, formal methods, and requirements traceability.
Praxiology as bounded gate-controlled execution leads to safety engineering, reliability engineering, and control theory.
Axiology as non-delegable professional responsibility leads to human factors and decision authority allocation.
Systems engineering is the principal means by which the four-pillar commitments are made architecturally real in Chirality.
The identified systems engineering disciplines are a coherent and defensible implementation of Chirality commitments, not the only possible implementation.
The architecture creates the conditions for knowledge, but it cannot create knowledge.
No architectural completeness can produce the professional commitment.
Facts cannot enact warranting.
The double commitment is an act of a person, not a consequence of a system.
The architecture makes professional commitment tractable by making warrant states visible, gaps surfaced, conflicts routed to decision-makers, and approvals bound to content.
Tractable commitment is not automatic commitment.
The professional must still look, judge, and commit.
The system can ensure the professional can commit, but it cannot ensure they do commit.
AI agents can produce claims with warrants.
AI agents can classify epistemic status, surface gaps and conflicts, generate semantic structures, and audit work-product warrant state.
AI agents cannot authenticate, take responsibility, or enact the commitment that transforms information into knowledge.
The inability of AI agents to authenticate is a consequence of what knowledge means in professional practice, not a current model limitation.
Knowledge requires an accountable self: a person who is identifiable, liable, and willing to be held to their warrant.
The gap between AI output and professional knowledge is structural rather than technological.
The gap between AI output and professional knowledge cannot be closed from the AI side.
Scaling, alignment, and self-assessed confidence do not produce accountability.
A model that never hallucinates still does not produce knowledge.
Knowledge is warranted information, and warranting is an act of a person under duty of care.
K-AUTH-1 says only humans author binding approval records, and the framework treats it as an ontological claim about professional knowledge.
Productivity tools optimize for output quality by making agent output better.
Professional accountability tools optimize for knowing what can be relied on.
Professional accountability tools make every claim epistemic status transparent so a competent professional can determine what to warrant.
Only the professional accountability approach supports the act that constitutes knowledge.
Knowledge is constituted by a qualified person committing to a claim on inspectable grounds under duty of care.
The Chirality Framework provides a rigorous structural implementation of conditions for professional commitment with AI-produced claims.
The framework addresses claims produced by AI agents, organized through project-management structures, and governed under explicit authority.
The Chirality axiom is to know what you know, why you know it, and why you know why.
The first clause of the axiom is ontological: identify the claims.
The second clause of the axiom is epistemic: verify the warrants.
The third clause of the axiom is reflexive: ensure the accountability structure itself is inspectable.
The reflexive clause makes knowledge professional rather than personal.
Professional knowledge can withstand scrutiny because the chain from claim to warrant to commitment is architecturally visible.
AI can accelerate professional work but cannot inherit professional responsibility.
The gap between acceleration and responsibility is the positive space where professional responsibility lives.
The gap between acceleration and responsibility is where a person assesses grounds and commits to what was produced.
Without the responsibility gap there is no space for commitment, and without commitment there is no knowledge.
The Chirality Framework holds the responsibility gap open and makes it workable.
The framework provides architecture for a professional to direct AI agents, review outputs, and authenticate results under duty of care with an auditable record.
If work cannot be made auditable, it cannot be relied on.
If work cannot be warranted, it is not knowledge.
The architecture makes work auditable, and the professional makes it knowledge.

A derivative package is assembled from accepted upstream truth.
Derivative packages must cite their upstream snapshot.
Derivative packages must never substitute for decomposition truth.
Every phase-boundary decision must produce an immutable snapshot.
Later phases consume accepted snapshots instead of mutable working state.
Agents have explicit, bounded write scopes.
Skills must never widen scope beyond what the agent shell and brief allow.
Claims carry `FACT`, `ASSUMPTION`, `PROPOSAL`, or `TBD` labels.
`TBD` markers are surfaced, not silently resolved.

UnitStatement: CONTRACT is the authoritative catalog of binding invariants for the Chirality project execution system.
Binding invariants are enforceable constraints for agents and tooling and human processes.
Each binding invariant includes an enforcement point describing where and how compliance is checked.
Invariant IDs using the K-* form are stable and never reused.
Retired invariants are moved to section 3 with retirement rationale.
Section 1 lists all K-* identifiers defined in the invariant catalog with their definition locations.
The invariant catalog defines 21 stable invariants across 10 subsections.
Projects are decomposed as flat packages containing deliverables with no nesting and no phases layer.
K-HIER-1 is enforced through PROJECT_DECOMP gates and PREPARATION folder creation and human review.
Deliverable IDs are stable and persist across path changes.
A deliverable path is a physical projection of decomposition and is not identity.
K-ID-1 is enforced by PROJECT_DECOMP ID assignment and by all agents when referencing IDs.
Only humans author binding approval records.
Agents may not claim to certify or approve or sign or seal or issue work for reliance.
K-AUTH-1 is enforced by agent instruction constraints and human review.
Approvals bind to a specific git SHA.
A content change after approval voids the approval.
K-AUTH-2 is enforced by human review and future SHA comparison tooling.
Approvals are always binding and only binding.
Non-binding guidance is allowed outside approval records.
K-BIND-1 is enforced by human process discipline.
Type 2 agent execution is forbidden before context is sealed and gate-approved by a human.
K-SEAL-1 is enforced by ORCHESTRATOR seal checks and human gate approval.
Type 2 agent context is limited to folder contents and declared references.
Ghost inputs are forbidden for Type 2 agent context.
K-GHOST-1 is enforced by agent instruction constraints for WRITE_SCOPE and _REFERENCES.md and by human review of diffs.
Deliverable-local _DEPENDENCIES.md and Dependencies.csv are authoritative for dependencies.
There is no central dependency graph.
Dependency aggregation occurs on demand via _Reconciliation/.
K-DEP-1 is enforced by TASK+dependency-extract local writes and read-only RECONCILIATION aggregation.
Dependency references to deliverables must resolve to existing deliverable IDs.
Unresolvable dependency targets use TargetType=UNKNOWN.
K-DEP-2 is enforced by TASK+dependency-extract Function 2 and validation checks.
_STATUS.md is the canonical human-readable lifecycle state file for each deliverable.
No file other than _STATUS.md determines deliverable state.
K-STATUS-1 is enforced by all agents reading _STATUS.md and transition rules in SPEC.md Section 3.3.
Upstream changes propagate staleness to all transitive dependent deliverables.
K-STALE-1 is enforced by future staleness calculation tooling and human triage.
Stale items must be triaged by a human before being considered current.
Stale item resolution modes are no impact clear flag and needs rework and needs review.
K-STALE-2 is enforced by the human triage queue.
A deliverable is dirty if any governed input has changed since its last approved SHA.
K-VAL-1 is enforced by future SHA comparison tooling and human review.
Gates are dynamic per project instance.
Minimum required gates are seal transition and pipeline run approval.
Additional gates are project-configurable.
K-GATE-1 is enforced by the ORCHESTRATOR gate map and human configuration.
Merge to main is allowed only when branch HEAD equals the approved SHA for the relevant run.
K-MERGE-1 is enforced by human review and a future CI check.
Every non-trivial governed claim must cite evidence with a source path and best-effort section reference or carry explicit location TBD.
Dependency rows are a schema-specific instance of the provenance rule.
Dependency rows use EvidenceFile and SourceRef under SPEC.md Section 6.5.
K-PROV-1 is enforced by agent instruction constraints and TASK+dependency-extract row validation and governance audits and human review.
Unknown values become TBD and are not guessed.
Agents must not invent scope items or dependency targets or parameter values or engineering content.
K-INVENT-1 is enforced by all agent instruction invariants and human review.
Conflicts between sources must be surfaced and not silently resolved.
Agents expose disagreements with pointers to the conflicting sources.
K-CONFLICT-1 is enforced by agent instruction invariants and human adjudication.
Claims and conclusions and characterizations must not overstate what the available warrant supports.
Statements of necessity and sufficiency and universality and completeness and exclusivity and direct regulatory conclusiveness require cited evidence that supports that strength.
Unsupported strong claims must be framed as interpretation or implementation-specific design or proposal.
K-CLAIM-1 is enforced by agent instruction constraints and governance audits and human review.
Every agent has an explicit write scope declared in its header block.
Agents do not write outside their declared zone.
K-WRITE-1 is enforced by the Agent Type table WRITE_SCOPE property and human review of diffs.
Task agent outputs to tool roots are immutable snapshots.
Pointer files named _LATEST.md may be overwritten.
Snapshot folders must not be overwritten.
K-SNAP-1 is enforced by agent instruction constraints and SPEC.md Section 11.
Agent instructions design-time checks constrain intent but do not guarantee behavior.
Agent instructions check K-GHOST-1 and K-WRITE-1 and K-SNAP-1 and K-PROV-1 and K-INVENT-1 and K-CONFLICT-1 and K-CLAIM-1 and K-DEP-1 and K-DEP-2.
ORCHESTRATOR runtime checks cover K-SEAL-1 and K-GATE-1 and K-HIER-1.
Human review gate checks cover K-AUTH-1 and K-AUTH-2 and K-BIND-1 and K-STALE-2 and K-MERGE-1 and K-VAL-1 and K-STATUS-1.
Future automated tooling checks cover K-STALE-1 and K-VAL-1 and K-MERGE-1 and K-AUTH-2 and K-DEP-2.
PROJECT_DECOMP decomposition checks cover K-HIER-1 and K-ID-1.
No invariants have been retired.
This DBM establishes the architectural basis for the governed workflow-component system shipped with the Chirality App.
The DBM governs how agents, skills, and tools are designed, related to each other, and kept coherent at scale.
The DBM audience includes people who work with, extend, audit, or maintain the agent instruction suite, skill subsystem, or deterministic tool layer.
The DBM scope includes the indexed agent suite described in AGENTS.md, including the two Type 0 canonical standards.
The DBM scope includes the repo-native skill subsystem under skills, governed by SKILLMAKER under HELPS_HUMANS.
The DBM scope includes the deterministic tool layer under tools, governed by TOOLMAKER under HELPS_HUMANS.
The DBM excludes the desktop application runtime, harness SDK, and UI from its workflow-component architecture scope.
DIRECTIVE.md supplies founding intent and design philosophy that this DBM operationalizes into the agent instruction layer.
SPEC.md defines filesystem contracts that agents write to, while this DBM defines the agents themselves.
TYPES.md defines domain vocabulary, ID formats, and enums, while this DBM defines how agents use them.
CONTRACT.md defines the K-* invariant catalog that this DBM maps to enforcing agents.
AGENTS.md is the operator-facing quick reference, while this DBM is the detailed architectural basis.
SE_Design_Analysis.md characterizes the systems engineering disciplines realized by the instruction architecture.
PROFESSIONAL_ENGINEERING.md traces the instruction architecture to APEGA regulatory obligations.
The agent instruction architecture is governed by eight foundational principles derived from DIRECTIVE.md.
The eight foundational principles form a structural dependency chain rather than independent guidelines.
The eight foundational principles operationalize ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology into the instruction layer.
The architecture identifies evidence-first knowledge architecture as its most distinctive load-bearing contribution.
Project truth lives in git-tracked files.
Agents must not maintain hidden databases, private state, or transient context that diverges from the filesystem.
Information that is not on disk does not exist for purposes of reliance.
V-model traceability, immutable snapshots, change propagation tracking, content-addressed approval, and audit trail capabilities depend on state being in git-tracked files.
Moving project state to a database would require rebuilding the filesystem-dependent systems engineering apparatus.
Humans own acceptance, rulings, conflict resolution, scope boundary changes, and publication approval.
Agents execute bounded work and preserve provenance, but they may propose and do not declare truth.
Every non-trivial claim includes a source path and best-effort section reference or an explicit location TBD.
Epistemic labels FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, and TBD distinguish observed, inferred, proposed, and unresolved content.
Mandatory provenance, no invention, and conflict surfacing collectively enforce the evidence-first response to hallucination risk.
The architecture treats gaps in evidence as findings rather than hidden failures.
When required information is missing, agents label it TBD and surface the gap as an open issue.
Agents do not guess, default-fill, or silently infer missing data.
Every agent declares an explicit write scope.
Tool roots for derived outputs are isolated from source truth where human-accepted deliverables live.
No agent writes outside its declared scope.
Write quarantine creates formal fault containment zones so Type 2 agent failures cannot corrupt source truth.
The system separates standards definition, interactive orchestration, and bounded task execution into Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 layers.
Each agent type layer has distinct responsibilities, constraints, and interaction patterns.
Task agents that produce analysis outputs write to timestamped snapshot folders that are never modified after creation.
Mutable pointer files provide convenience access to the most recent immutable snapshot.
The snapshot trail is the audit trail.
Structure is added only when it reduces error or rework.
Rigor scales with stakes while avoiding premature abstraction and unnecessary ceremony.
The agent system is organized into three types with distinct responsibilities, constraints, and interaction patterns.
Type 0 agents define invariant protocols and design standards that downstream agents must conform to.
Type 0 agents do not write project state and form the constitutional layer.
HELPS_HUMANS defines agent header blocks, R1-R12 compliance, four-section structure, brief formats, QA contract, publication hygiene, and skill/tool design outcomes.
DECOMP_BASE defines the decomposition 7-gate protocol, I1-I10 invariants, entity schemas, extension contract, and ledger and telemetry contracts.
Any AGENT_* file, skill contract, or tool contract that disagrees with a Type 0 standard must be edited to conform.
SKILLMAKER is a Type 1 manager that governs the repo-native skill subsystem under HELPS_HUMANS requirements.
TOOLMAKER is a Type 1 manager that governs the deterministic-tool layer under HELPS_HUMANS requirements.
Skills identify tool needs, while tools implement deterministic helpers.
Type 2 agents cannot initiate gate reviews, spawn other agents, or make scope decisions.
Type 1 agents cannot relax Type 0 constraints such as R1-R12, I1-I10, or K-* invariants.
No agent can bypass human gates to approve deliverables, issue work for reliance, resolve conflicts authoritatively, or commit to the baseline.
Type 1 agents are human-facing personas that run conversational gate-controlled workflows.
Type 1 agents use AGENT_CLASS PERSONA, chat interaction, and allowed blocking.
Type 1 agents run multi-phase workflows with explicit gate questions at each phase.
Type 1 agents may spawn Type 2 agents and own orchestration decisions but not engineering content.
Type 1 agents produce guidance, run plans, briefs, and structured cards.
Type 2 agents are brief-driven specialists that run straight-through without human interaction.
Type 2 agents receive structured inputs, produce auditable outputs, and return status to the invoking agent.
Type 2 agents use AGENT_CLASS TASK, INIT-TASK or spawned interaction, and never blocking.
Type 2 agents produce immutable snapshots or deliverable-local file writes.
Type 2 agents never spawn other agents.
Type 2 agents halt with FAILED_INPUTS for invalid inputs and continue conservatively with TBD for missing data.
Every agent instruction file follows a universal skeleton mandated by AGENT_HELPS_HUMANS.md.
Agent instruction files begin with YAML frontmatter containing a one-line description for UI labels.
Agent instruction files include a DOC marker, title, AGENT_TYPE declaration, Agent Type table, precedence order, invariants, and four delimited sections.
The top-level agent heading names the agent and role description.
Each agent instruction file declares AGENT_TYPE immediately after the title block.
The Agent Type table records AGENT_TYPE, AGENT_CLASS, INTERACTION_SURFACE, WRITE_SCOPE, BLOCKING, and PRIMARY_OUTPUTS.
Agent instruction precedence orders conflicts as PROTOCOL before SPEC, SPEC before STRUCTURE, and STRUCTURE before RATIONALE.
Agent instruction files include five to fourteen non-negotiable invariants.
The PROTOCOL section governs operational workflow steps, phases, gates, or functions.
The SPEC section governs validity requirements and invalid states.
The STRUCTURE section governs file schemas, templates, and output formats.
The RATIONALE section records non-normative design intent.
The Agent Header Block has six required fields.
AGENT_TYPE records the agent position in the Type 0, Type 1, or Type 2 hierarchy.
AGENT_CLASS records whether the agent has a conversational persona interface or task interface.
INTERACTION_SURFACE records how the agent is invoked.
WRITE_SCOPE records what filesystem area the agent may write to.
BLOCKING records whether the agent may pause for human input.
PRIMARY_OUTPUTS records what the agent produces.
The four standard sections are PROTOCOL, SPEC, STRUCTURE, and RATIONALE.
PROTOCOL has the highest precedence because it governs sequencing and interaction rules.
SPEC has second precedence because it defines pass/fail validity requirements.
STRUCTURE has third precedence because it defines allowed entities, relationships, schemas, and templates.
RATIONALE has the lowest precedence because it interprets ambiguity through design values and intent.
All standard sections are bounded by BEGIN and END delimiters for machine parseability.
Type 1 PROTOCOL sections use multi-phase gated workflows with human gates.
Type 2 PROTOCOL sections use straight-through numbered steps without mid-run gates.
Type 1 inputs use natural language conversation, while Type 2 inputs use a structured INIT-TASK brief.
Type 1 outputs are conversational guidance and structured cards, while Type 2 outputs are file writes and PASS/FAIL run reports.
Type 1 agents may spawn Type 2 agents, while Type 2 agents never spawn others.
Three complementary and non-overlapping layers of contracts govern agent behavior.
R1 requires human-owned decisions to be enumerated and preserved.
R2 requires task agents to run without mid-run human decisions.
R3 requires every agent to have an explicit write scope and isolates tool roots from source truth.
R4 requires each run to produce a new immutable snapshot folder while allowing pointer files to be overwritten.
R5 requires aggregated or extracted data to include SourcePath and a best-effort SectionRef.
R6 requires no-invention behavior where missing data becomes TBD with assumptions captured.
R7 requires conflicts and duplicates to be surfaced rather than hidden or silently resolved.
R8 requires pipelines to have defined INIT-TASK brief formats and deterministic outputs.
R9 requires version-control publishing to be reviewable and non-destructive by default.
R10 requires every skill to declare tool policy, fallbacks, and disallowed tools.
R11 requires every deterministic tool to declare input/output contracts, scope boundaries, and idempotence posture.
R12 preserves the skill/tool boundary by keeping tool needs in skills and deterministic helper implementation in tools.
I1 requires decomposition to be human-validated at defined gates.
I2 prohibits creating units, objectives, or artifacts beyond source material and maps unknowns to TBD.
I3 requires decomposition partitions to be flat rather than nested.
I4 requires every IN-scope atomic unit to be assigned to exactly one partition without overlaps or gaps.
I5 requires stable identifiers unless a human explicitly requests renumbering.
I6 requires production unit IDs to be mechanically derived from parent partition IDs.
I7 requires objective mapping to be best-effort with unmapped objectives surfaced as open issues.
I8 requires non-trivial assignment decisions to have explicit traceable rationale.
I9 requires every decomposition to include a machine-checkable ledger and Coverage and Telemetry summary.
I10 requires every decomposition to include a Vocabulary Map with consistent canonical terms.
K-HIER-1 and K-ID-1 are enforced primarily by PROJECT_DECOMP and PREPARATION.
K-AUTH-1, K-AUTH-2, and K-BIND-1 are enforced primarily by REVIEW and CHANGE approval gates.
K-SEAL-1 and K-GHOST-1 are enforced by Type 2 agents checking lifecycle state before writes.
K-DEP-1 and K-DEP-2 are enforced primarily by TASK+dependency-extract and AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE.
K-STATUS-1 is enforced by PREPARATION, TASK+four-documents, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, and REVIEW.
K-STALE-1, K-STALE-2, and K-VAL-1 are enforced by AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE, RECONCILIATION, and future SHA tooling.
K-GATE-1 is enforced primarily by ORCHESTRATOR and SCHEDULING.
K-MERGE-1 is enforced by CHANGE.
K-PROV-1 is universally enforced by all claim-producing agents.
K-INVENT-1 is universally enforced by all agents.
K-CONFLICT-1 is universally enforced by all agents.
K-WRITE-1 is enforced through every agent WRITE_SCOPE declaration.
K-SNAP-1 is enforced by all snapshot-producing agents.
MUST and MUST NOT are mandatory for compliance in agent instructions.
SHOULD and SHOULD NOT indicate recommended best practice in agent instructions.
MAY indicates optional behavior in agent instructions.
AGENTS.md is the canonical agent registry for active membership, matrix placement, role classification, and TASK dispatch relationships.
Skills are discovered through skills/README.md and live skills/*/SKILL.md files.
Deterministic tools are registered in tools/REGISTRY.md.
Test surfaces are generated on demand by tools/validation/discover_test_surfaces.py.
The orchestration architecture defines spawning and dispatch relationships among workflow agents.
HELP_HUMAN classifies intent and routes to agents but does not spawn agents.
ORCHESTRATOR spawns PREPARATION, DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH for DOMAIN Phase 2.6, ESTIMATING, and AGGREGATION.
ORCHESTRATOR dispatches TASK+four-documents, TASK+domain-documents, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, TASK+lens-register, TASK+dependency-extract, estimate-snapshot, and estimate-prep skills.
WORKING_ITEMS spawns TASK agents.
RECONCILIATION spawns AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE, AUDIT_AGENTS, AUDIT_DECOMP, and DOMAIN-only AUDIT_HYPERGRAPH_CLOSURE.
EVALUATION spawns CONTENT_DIGEST, EVALUATION_REPORT, EVALUATION_STRUCTURE_AUDIT, and EVALUATION_DEPENDENCY_AUDIT.
DBM_PUBLISHER dispatches TASK+dbm-section-publish for one approved section per run and TASK+dbm-publish for package assembly and readiness gate.
CHANGE is a leaf agent that spawns nothing and implements approved edits.
REVIEW triggers AUDIT_DECOMP as a precondition check.
SCOPE_CHANGE hands off to ORCHESTRATOR for PREPARATION and CHANGE for commits.
CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE hands off to CHANGE for publication.
SCHEDULING is standalone and reads dependency graphs to produce schedule artifacts.
TOOLMAKER is standalone and designs and implements deterministic tools before handing off to CHANGE for publication.
SKILLMAKER is standalone and governs skills while coordinating with TOOLMAKER for deterministic helpers.
PDF2MD spawns PDF2MD_PAGE per page.
PDF2MD optionally spawns PDF2MD_PAGE_ASSETS per page when ASSET_MODE is prose.
DRAWING_EXTRACT spawns DRAWING_EXTRACT_PAGE per page.
The system maintains session continuity across agent invocations through durable NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md and NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md artifacts.
NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md is created by ORCHESTRATOR, is stable unless protocol changes, and contains stable session startup instructions.
NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md is created by ORCHESTRATOR, updated by WORKING_ITEMS at handoff, and records current pointers, program state, active rulings, and immediate next actions.
The session handoff flow is ORCHESTRATOR creation, WORKING_ITEMS startup read, WORKING_ITEMS end-of-session update, and CHANGE verification before commit.
Human-gated phases let ORCHESTRATOR run sequential phases with human confirmation between each phase.
Pre-authorized dispatch lets WORKING_ITEMS dispatch TASK agents autonomously after human confirmation of the session objective.
Human-directed toolbelts let RECONCILIATION dispatch only agents listed in the human-provided TOOLBELT.
RECONCILIATION uses a formal 9-field brief schema and defaults to at most one task per cycle.
Approval-gated execution requires CHANGE to receive explicit APPROVE or APPROVE_DESTRUCTIVE tokens before any state-changing action.
The write scope architecture enforces separation between source truth and derived outputs.
NONE write scope is read-only and may draft content for a human to apply.
HELPS_HUMANS, DECOMP_BASE, and HELP_HUMAN use NONE write scope.
REPO-METADATA-ONLY scope covers instruction files, README files, and templates, but not execution truth.
DOMAIN_DECOMP and CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE use REPO-METADATA-ONLY write scope.
REPO-WIDE scope covers tools, skills, and related contract documents.
PROJECT-LEVEL scope covers decomposition documents, metadata files, and folder scaffolding.
DELIVERABLE-LOCAL scope is limited to a single production unit folder.
TASK shell writes are bounded by the selected skill under TASK hard scope.
TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope restricts agents to derived output roots under the execution root.
Publication-local TASK skills write under publication-bounded scopes in _Publication/DBM.
Every agent declares its write scope in the Agent Header Block.
Deliverable-local agents cannot write outside their assigned production unit folder.
Tool-root agents write only to their designated tool root under the execution root.
Tool-root agents never modify source truth deliverable production documents.
_STATUS.md updates are restricted to designated actors and only for forward lifecycle transitions.
WORKING_ITEMS sessions prohibit cross-deliverable scanning or editing unless the human explicitly requests a cross-check.
The decomposition system is governed by DECOMP_BASE protocol, outputs, ledger, variants, and extension contracts.
All decomposition agents conform to an invariant 7-gate conversational workflow.
Phase 1 Intake captures source material faithfully and asks whether the source material and context are reflected as intended.
Phase 2 Normalize converts source material into atomic units and vocabulary and asks whether units, classifications, and vocabulary are correct.
Phase 3 Objectives derives success criteria from source and asks whether the objectives represent success as intended.
Phase 4 Partitions creates flat groupings with no nesting, overlaps, or gaps and asks whether each IN-scope unit belongs to exactly one partition.
Phase 5 Production Units operationalizes each partition into bounded work units and asks whether granularity, types, and responsibilities are acceptable.
Phase 6 Coverage proves completeness, surfaces gaps, and asks whether mappings and open issues are acceptable.
Phase 7 Publish finalizes the accepted decomposition basis for downstream work.
Every decomposition document must include a Vocabulary Map.
Every decomposition document must include a machine-checkable Decomposition Ledger.
Every decomposition document must include Coverage and Telemetry counts, gap metrics, and open issue taxonomy.
Every decomposition document must include unresolved Open Issues referencing stable IDs.
Every decomposition document must include a Decision Log for non-trivial assignment decisions.
The Decomposition Ledger minimum columns are UnitID, InOutStatus, UnitStatement, SourceRef, PartitionID, ProductionUnitID(s), ObjectiveID(s), DecisionRef, OpenIssue, and Notes.
Every IN-scope UnitID in the Decomposition Ledger has exactly one PartitionID.
PROJECT_DECOMP applies to EPC or design-build domains using SOW source corpus and SSOW structured outline.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP applies to software development domains using SOW source corpus and SSOW structured outline.
DOMAIN_DECOMP applies to handbook or knowledge domains using handbook source corpus and SDO structured outline.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP atomic units are scope items, while DOMAIN_DECOMP atomic units are handbook units.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP partitions are packages, while DOMAIN_DECOMP partitions are categories.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP production units are deliverables, while DOMAIN_DECOMP production units are knowledge types.
PROJECT_DECOMP deliverable IDs derive their first three digits from package digits.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP deliverable IDs derive their first two digits from package digits.
DOMAIN_DECOMP KTY identifiers derive category and type indexes from CAT and type numbering.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP use fixed four-document production sets.
DOMAIN_DECOMP uses variable Knowledge Artifacts as production documents.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP include dependency graphs, while DOMAIN_DECOMP does not.
PROJECT_DECOMP requires discipline-exclusive design packages.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP requires mandatory S, M, L, or XL Context Envelope sizing.
DOMAIN_DECOMP requires canonical knowledge schemas across five types.
A conforming decomposition agent must reference AGENT_DECOMP_BASE.md and state conformance.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide an entity binding table from abstract terms to domain-specific terms.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide ID formats and width specifications.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide a production unit type taxonomy.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide phase-specific extensions for domain actions, outputs, and gate language.
A conforming decomposition agent must declare WRITE_SCOPE.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide domain-specific fields, anti-patterns, and SPEC requirements.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide domain-specific telemetry fields.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP can extend any branch that has software to build and can recursively extend other SOFTWARE_DECOMP branches.
DOMAIN_DECOMP captures the knowledge domain a branch operates within and can recursively parallel other DOMAIN_DECOMP branches.
Brief and output contracts define how Type 2 work is initialized and how run artifacts are produced.
All Type 2 agents accept a structured brief supplied inline or through a file-based INIT-TASK.md control surface.
When inline brief fields and file-derived brief fields are both present, inline fields are authoritative.
The recommended INIT-TASK template includes purpose, optional path, scope, where-to-look roots, output label, config, constraints, exclusions, and notes.
Publication-local TASK dispatches should use ScopePath and AllowedWriteTargets inside the DBM publication execution root.
Section publication runs should point to sections/{SectionID}, and package publication runs should point to package snapshots.
PREPARATION brief extensions include task type and PKG_ID, DEL_ID, CAT_ID, and KTY_ID identifiers.
TASK+four-documents brief extensions include deliverable path, decomposition reference, run passes, overwrite states, and decomposition variant.
TASK+domain-documents brief extensions include KTY path, unit scope, artifact naming, and maximum artifacts.
TASK+dbm-section-publish brief extensions include section identity, publication manifests, schema paths, rules, concordance register, and maximum KA files.
TASK+dbm-publish brief extensions include publication root, input manifest, schema, section map, rules, concordance register, sections root, and package output root.
TASK+dependency-extract brief extensions include mode, strictness, consumer context, and source documents.
TASK+semantic-matrix-build brief extensions include deliverable folder and decomposition variant.
TASK+lens-register brief extensions include deliverable folder and decomposition variant.
ESTIMATING brief extensions include basis of estimate, currency, and price sources.
ESTIMATE_PREP brief extensions include phase, project context, and human pricing.
AGGREGATION brief extensions include purpose, pipeline ID, and currency normalization policy.
TASK brief extensions include InitTaskPath, ScopePath or DeliverablePath, TaskProfile, TaskSkill, AllowedTools, RuntimeOverrides, and CustomInstructions.
DELIVERABLE_TASK brief extensions include deliverable path, edit application mode, semantic lensing, and permission flags.
AUDIT_AGENTS brief extensions include files to audit, canonical file, and rubric file.
AUDIT_DECOMP brief extensions include decomposition path, decomposition variant, and scope.
AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE brief extensions include scope, edge filter, and hub threshold.
DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH brief extensions include execution root, CAT or KTY scope, decomposition path, ledger path, and objective map path.
AUDIT_HYPERGRAPH_CLOSURE brief extensions include hypergraph reference, required ledger checks, and strict mode.
RECONCILIATION defines a formal 9-field schema for all Type 2 dispatches.

The deliverable lifecycle is a formal state machine with authorized transition actors.
The lifecycle path proceeds from OPEN to INITIALIZED to SEMANTIC_READY to IN_PROGRESS to CHECKING to ISSUED.
PREPARATION authorizes the OPEN to INITIALIZED transition.
TASK+four-documents or TASK+domain-documents authorizes the INITIALIZED to SEMANTIC_READY transition.
TASK+semantic-matrix-build authorizes the SEMANTIC_READY to IN_PROGRESS transition.
A human authorizes the IN_PROGRESS to CHECKING transition.
REVIEW plus human approval authorizes the CHECKING to ISSUED transition.
K-STATUS-1 makes _STATUS.md the canonical state indicator.
Lifecycle transitions are forward-only under normal operation.
Each lifecycle transition is recorded in append-only History with date, actor, and rationale.

Humans own hazard and risk acceptance.
Humans own conflict adjudication and rulings.
Humans own approval, issuance, and signature.

The valid lifecycle state sequence is OPEN to INITIALIZED to SEMANTIC_READY to IN_PROGRESS to CHECKING to ISSUED.
OPEN means the folder exists but has no content yet, typically triggered by PREPARATION creating the folder.
INITIALIZED means draft documents have been generated, typically triggered when TASK+four-documents completes the document kit.
SEMANTIC_READY means the semantic lens has been generated, typically triggered by TASK+semantic-matrix-build writing _SEMANTIC.md.
IN_PROGRESS means active human and agent work has begun.
CHECKING means the deliverable is under review after a human moves it to review.
ISSUED means the deliverable has been released after human approval and issue.
PREPARATION is authorized to transition a deliverable into OPEN.
TASK+four-documents is authorized to transition a deliverable from OPEN to INITIALIZED.
TASK+semantic-matrix-build is authorized to transition a deliverable from INITIALIZED to SEMANTIC_READY.
A human or WORKING_ITEMS may transition a deliverable from INITIALIZED to IN_PROGRESS when the semantic step is skipped.
A human or WORKING_ITEMS may transition a deliverable from SEMANTIC_READY to IN_PROGRESS.
Only a human is authorized to transition a deliverable from IN_PROGRESS to CHECKING.
Only a human is authorized to transition a deliverable from CHECKING to ISSUED.
_STATUS.md is the authoritative lifecycle indicator for deliverable state.
No file other than _STATUS.md determines deliverable state.
Stage gates such as 30, 60, 90, or IFC are human-managed milestones and are not lifecycle states.
Stage gates are tracked separately in coordination records.
_CONTEXT.md header fields must match the decomposition document exactly.
The Decomposition Reference in _CONTEXT.md must point to the specific decomposition document used.
_CONTEXT.md is created by PREPARATION and must not be modified by agents other than through permitted human edits.
_DEPENDENCIES.md is a hybrid container with human-owned and agent-owned zones.
PREPARATION creates the human-owned dependency sections, and humans or ORCHESTRATOR maintain them.
Human-owned dependency sections include Dependency Tracking Mode, Declared Upstream, and Declared Downstream.
TASK+dependency-extract populates the agent-owned dependency sections.
Agent-owned dependency sections include Extracted Dependency Register, Run Notes and History, Lifecycle Summary, and Consumer Handoff Notes.
The Dependency Tracking Mode field accepts NOT_TRACKED, DECLARED, or TRACKED.
_DEPENDENCIES.md points to Dependencies.csv using schema v3.1.
NOT_TRACKED means dependencies are coordinated externally by humans.
DECLARED means only human-declared upstream and downstream dependencies are tracked, with no agent extraction.
TRACKED means full extraction is performed via TASK+dependency-extract and Dependencies.csv is present.

The DependencyID column is required and must be unique within the deliverable register.

The FromDeliverableName column is required and stores the human-readable name of the host deliverable.
The DependencyClass column is required and must be ANCHOR or EXECUTION.
The AnchorType column is required and uses the canonical enum values defined in Section 6.3.
The Direction column is required and must be UPSTREAM or DOWNSTREAM.
The DependencyType column is required and uses the canonical enum values defined in Section 6.3.
The TargetType column is required and uses the canonical enum values defined in Section 6.3.
The TargetPackageID column is optional and stores the target package ID when the target is a deliverable.
The TargetDeliverableID column is optional and stores the stable deliverable ID when TargetType is DELIVERABLE.
The TargetRefID column is optional and stores a stable reference ID for non-deliverable targets.
The TargetName column should provide a human-readable target name or description.
The TargetLocation column optionally stores a path, URL, or document identifier for the target.
The Statement column should provide a human-readable dependency statement.
The EvidenceFile column must identify the source document containing evidence or use location TBD.
The SourceRef column must provide a path plus heading or section within the evidence file, or use location TBD.
The EvidenceQuote column should provide a traceability quote of no more than 30 words.
The Explicitness column should classify a dependency as EXPLICIT or IMPLICIT.
The RequiredMaturity column optionally records the maturity level required for dependency satisfaction.
The ProposedMaturity column optionally records an agent-suggested maturity level.
The SatisfactionStatus column should use the canonical satisfaction enum values defined in Section 6.3.
The Confidence column should classify evidence confidence as HIGH, MEDIUM, or LOW.

The FirstSeen column is required and uses the ISO YYYY-MM-DD date of first extraction.
The LastSeen column is required and uses the ISO YYYY-MM-DD date of most recent confirmation.
The Status column is required and must be ACTIVE or RETIRED.
The Notes column is optional and may include explanatory remarks or epistemic labels such as FACT, ASSUMPTION, or PROPOSAL.
Extension columns may be present in Dependencies.csv without breaking compatibility.
EstimateImpactClass is an extension column with values BLOCKING, ADVISORY, INFO, and TBD.
ConsumerHint is an extension column with values TASK, TASK_ESTIMATING, AGGREGATION, RECONCILIATION, and TBD.
ANCHOR is a DependencyClass value for tree edges that connect deliverables to definition or traceability nodes.
EXECUTION is a DependencyClass value for DAG edges representing information flow, prerequisites, handoffs, or constraints.
IMPLEMENTS_NODE is an AnchorType value for a parent definition node, with exactly one per deliverable.
TRACES_TO_REQUIREMENT is an AnchorType value for zero or more requirement trace links.
NOT_APPLICABLE is an AnchorType value used for EXECUTION rows.
UPSTREAM means the deliverable requires information from the target.
DOWNSTREAM means the deliverable produces information for the target.
PREREQUISITE is the preferred DependencyType for required input or approval before work can proceed.
INTERFACE is the preferred DependencyType for explicit data or artifact exchange between deliverables.
HANDOVER is the preferred DependencyType for output of one deliverable consumed as input to another.
CONSTRAINT is the preferred DependencyType for an explicit constraint or condition.
ENABLES is the preferred DependencyType when a deliverable enables downstream work.
OTHER is the preferred DependencyType for dependencies that do not fit other categories and for ANCHOR rows.
COORDINATION is a legacy DependencyType that must not be emitted in new extractions.
INFORMATION is a legacy DependencyType that must not be emitted directly in new extractions.
DELIVERABLE is a TargetType for another deliverable in the project.
PACKAGE is a TargetType for a package and is used in ANCHOR rows.
WBS_NODE is a TargetType for a work breakdown structure or scope node.
REQUIREMENT is a TargetType for a specific requirement such as a SOW item or objective.
DOCUMENT is a TargetType for an external or reference document.
EQUIPMENT is a TargetType for physical equipment or assets.
EXTERNAL is a TargetType for an external entity, organization, standard, or similar target.
UNKNOWN is a TargetType for targets that cannot be confidently resolved.
EXPLICIT means the dependency is directly stated in source text.
IMPLICIT means the dependency is implied but not directly stated.
TBD means SatisfactionStatus has not yet been assessed.
PENDING means SatisfactionStatus has been assessed but not yet satisfied.
IN_PROGRESS means SatisfactionStatus is actively being worked toward satisfaction.
SATISFIED means the dependency has been fulfilled.
WAIVED means the dependency was waived by human decision.
NOT_APPLICABLE means the dependency was determined not to be applicable.
HIGH confidence means strong evidence with an explicit source reference.
MEDIUM confidence means reasonable evidence with some interpretation required.
LOW confidence means weak evidence with significant interpretation or assumption.
DECLARED origin means the dependency was human-declared.
EXTRACTED origin means the dependency was extracted by an agent from source documents.
ACTIVE status means the dependency is currently observed and relevant.
RETIRED status means the dependency was previously observed but is no longer found in source text.
ANCHOR rows connect a deliverable to the project's definition tree.
Exactly one IMPLEMENTS_NODE row should exist per deliverable.
Zero or more TRACES_TO_REQUIREMENT rows may connect a deliverable to scope items, objectives, or requirements.
DependencyType must be OTHER for ANCHOR rows.
AnchorType must not be NOT_APPLICABLE for ANCHOR rows.
EXECUTION rows capture information flow and constraints.
EXECUTION rows must have DependencyClass set to EXECUTION.
EXECUTION rows must have AnchorType set to NOT_APPLICABLE.
EXECUTION rows use the preferred execution DependencyType enums PREREQUISITE, INTERFACE, HANDOVER, CONSTRAINT, ENABLES, and OTHER.
Every ACTIVE dependency row must include EvidenceFile identifying the source document or location TBD.
Every ACTIVE dependency row must include SourceRef identifying the path plus heading or section, or location TBD.
EvidenceQuote should be provided for traceability with a maximum of 30 words.
Each dependency row tracks an extraction lifecycle and a closure lifecycle.
The extraction lifecycle includes FirstSeen, LastSeen, and Status.
FirstSeen records the date the dependency row was first created.
LastSeen records the date the dependency row was most recently confirmed by extraction.
Status records whether a dependency row is ACTIVE or RETIRED in the extraction lifecycle.
The closure lifecycle includes RequiredMaturity, ProposedMaturity, and SatisfactionStatus.
RequiredMaturity records the maturity level needed for dependency satisfaction.
ProposedMaturity records the agent-suggested maturity level for dependency satisfaction.
SatisfactionStatus records the current satisfaction state of a dependency.
Dependency rows are never deleted.
Rows no longer observed in source text are marked RETIRED.
Legacy Direction value INBOUND normalizes to canonical UPSTREAM.
Legacy Direction value OUTBOUND normalizes to canonical DOWNSTREAM.
Legacy DependencyType value COORDINATION normalizes to canonical OTHER.
Legacy DependencyType value INFORMATION must be interpreted and mapped to PREREQUISITE, INTERFACE, HANDOVER, CONSTRAINT, or ENABLES as appropriate.

DependencyID uses the format DEP-{PKG}-{DEL}-{SEQ}.

When TargetType is DELIVERABLE, TargetDeliverableID must contain the target's stable deliverable ID.
For non-deliverable targets, TargetDeliverableID must be empty and TargetRefID and TargetName are used instead.
References are listed as relative paths where preferred, or as absolute paths to source documents.
Each reference entry includes a brief relevance statement.

All AGENT_*.md instruction files must follow the structure defined by AGENT_HELPS_HUMANS.md.
Agent instruction files require the [[DOC:AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS]] document tag in the header.
Agent instruction files require the title pattern AGENT INSTRUCTIONS - {AGENT_NAME} ({Brief Descriptor}).
Agent instruction files require an AGENT_TYPE body header with value 0, 1, or 2.
The Agent Type table records AGENT_TYPE, AGENT_CLASS, INTERACTION_SURFACE, WRITE_SCOPE, BLOCKING, and PRIMARY_OUTPUTS.

Every agent instruction file must include SPEC markers for validity requirements.
Every agent instruction file must include STRUCTURE markers for schemas, templates, and artifact definitions.

Use the role name when referring to the agent itself.
Harness runtime metadata parsing uses a split contract between YAML frontmatter and the canonical body header/table.
Runtime YAML frontmatter may provide description, subagents, tools, model, max_turns, disallowed_tools, and auto_approve_tools.
The canonical body header/table provides the AGENT_TYPE line and AGENT_CLASS value.
Delegated subagents must declare AGENT_TYPE: 2 in the body header.
AGENT_CLASS: TASK is preferred for delegated subagents and validated as a warning-level rule.
Runtime injects subagents only when CHIRALITY_ENABLE_SUBAGENTS is true and a Type 1 persona is allowlisted for subagents.
Runtime injects subagents only if opts.subagentGovernance is present and valid.
Valid subagentGovernance requires contextSealed to be true.
Valid subagentGovernance requires pipelineRunApproved to be true.
Valid subagentGovernance requires approvalRef to be a non-empty string.
approvedBy is optional in subagentGovernance metadata.
Missing or invalid governance metadata must block subagent injection while allowing the parent turn to continue normally.
POST /api/harness/turn accepts opts and applies runtime option mapping.
POST /api/harness/session/boot accepts opts while bootstrap policy remains authoritative for bootstrap-only constraints.
POST /api/harness/turn accepts optional attachments as an array of absolute filesystem path strings.
The UI sends attachment paths only; server-side runtime classifies and reads files.
Client-supplied attachment metadata is non-authoritative and must not be trusted for execution.
A turn may omit text when attachments are present.
Resolver validation is server-side and enforces supported attachment extensions.
Supported attachment extensions are .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .gif, .webp, .pdf, .txt, .md, and .csv.
Resolver validation rejects directories, symlinks, and special files by requiring stats.isFile().
Resolver validation enforces a 10 MB per-file size limit.
Resolver validation enforces an 18 MB total per-turn raw-byte budget.
Partial attachment failure is non-fatal when at least one attachment resolves or user text exists.
If all attachments fail and user text is empty, the request is rejected with 400.
When there are no attachments, runtime uses SDK query with a string prompt.
When attachments are present, runtime builds multimodal content blocks and uses SDK query with an AsyncIterable prompt.
The UI stores Attachment records for preview purposes only and the server reclassifies attachments.
On send failure, the UI rolls back the optimistic user message and streaming placeholder while preserving the draft and attachment selections.
Session rehydration validates attachment shape, silently drops malformed records, and restores valid records.
The UI may expose any subset of supported opts fields.
Omitted opts fields must follow runtime fallback chains.
UI visibility of a field must not be interpreted as runtime authorization.
Model selection falls back from opts.model to the global model to the runtime default.
Tool selection falls back from opts.tools to persona tools frontmatter to the runtime preset.
Max turns falls back from opts.maxTurns to persona max_turns frontmatter to the runtime default.
The UI may present delegation governance fields for operator use.
Runtime gate and seal logic remains authoritative for delegation governance.
Supplying opts.subagentGovernance does not guarantee delegation because all runtime gates must still pass.

Two claims may be in conflict when they share the same key, have incompatible values, and come from different sources.
A conflict requires a ruling.
HumanRuling remains TBD until the licensed professional adjudicates a conflict.
A ruling transforms status by resolving gaps, accepting or rejecting proposals, and resolving conflicts.
Resolving a gap changes status from TBD to FACT or ASSUMPTION.
Resolving a conflict changes competing claims into one accepted claim.
Four epistemic labels classify claim certainty status.
FACT means directly observed in source text with citation.
FACT reviewer action is to verify the citation and accept if the source is authoritative.
ASSUMPTION means reasonable inference grounded in cited material but not directly stated.
ASSUMPTION requires validation or rejection and a documented decision.
PROPOSAL means suggested interpretation, action, or design move.
PROPOSAL may cite supporting context.
PROPOSAL requires a human decision to become binding.
TBD means an unknown placeholder requiring resolution.
TBD must be resolved before reliance.
Claims within a deliverable progress through a warrant lifecycle.
The warrant lifecycle tracks epistemic state.
The warrant lifecycle is interleaved with the deliverable lifecycle.
The warrant lifecycle sequence is UNWARRANTED -> CITED -> REVIEWED -> AUTHENTICATED.
UNWARRANTED means a claim exists but has no source citation.
UNWARRANTED status is TBD or uncited PROPOSAL.
UNWARRANTED transition mechanism is agent claim production with K-INVENT-1 requiring TBD marking for gaps.
CITED means a claim has a source citation.
CITED status is FACT, ASSUMPTION, or cited PROPOSAL.
CITED transition mechanism is agent-attached provenance enforced by K-PROV-1.
REVIEWED means a claim has been examined by a licensed professional.
REVIEWED findings have been dispositioned.
REVIEWED transition mechanism is REVIEW gates and human rulings on findings.
AUTHENTICATED means a claim is part of an authenticated PWP.
In AUTHENTICATED state, the professional warrants the claim under duty of care.
AUTHENTICATED transition mechanism is authentication binding to git SHA enforced by K-AUTH-2.
The deliverable lifecycle asks what state the work product is in.
The warrant lifecycle asks what state the knowledge about the work product is in.

Transition to ISSUED requires professional authentication of the work.
Professional authentication warrants deliverable claims under professional responsibility.
K-PROV-1 mandatory provenance governs Warrant.
K-PROV-1 requires every claim to have an extrinsic warrant or explicit location TBD.
K-INVENT-1 no invention governs Gap.
K-INVENT-1 requires missing data to be represented as a gap, not fabricated.

K-CONFLICT-1 requires disagreements to be exposed as conflicts, not silently resolved.
